title: Cu2−xS derived copper nanoparticles: A platform for unraveling the role of surface reconstruction in efficient electrocatalytic CO2-to-C2H4 conversion
abstract: Cu-based electrocatalysts have provoked much attention for their high activity and selectivity in carbon dioxide (CO2) conversion into multi-carbon hydrocarbons. However, during the electrochemical reaction, Cu catalysts inevitably undergo surface reconstruction whose impact on CO2 conversion performance remains contentious. Here we report that polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles (denoted as Cu-s) with rich high-index facets, derived from Cu2−xS through desulphurization and surface reconstruction, offer an excellent platform for investigating the role of surface reconstruction in electrocatalytic CO2 conversion. During the formation of Cu-s catalyst, the two stages of desulphurization and surface reconstruction can be clearly resolved by in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy and OH adsorption characterizations, which are well correlated with the changes in electrocatalytic performance. It turns out that the high CO2 conversion performance, achieved by the Cu-s catalyst (Faradic efficiency of 68.6% and partial current density of 40.8 mA/cm in H-cell toward C2H4 production), is attributed to the increased percentage of high-index facets in Cu-s during the surface reconstruction. Furthermore, the operando electrochemical Raman spectroscopy further reveals that the conversion of the CO2 into the C2H4 on Cu-s is intermediated by the production of *COCHO. Our findings manifest that the surface reconstruction is an effective method for tuning the reaction intermediate of the CO2 conversion toward high-value multicarbon (C2+) chemicals, and highlight the significance of in situ characterizations in enhancing the understanding of the surface structure and its role in electrocatalysis.

sections.text: KEYWORDS CO2 electroreduction reaction, surface reconstruction, high-index facets, ethylene (C2H4), Cu catalysts

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The sharp rise of carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration in the atmosphere along with the increasing demand for fossil fuels is two major challenges for humankind in this century. In this regard, tremendous attention has been devoted to utilize the reclaimed CO2 from the atmosphere as a carbon feedstock and convert it into high-value industrial chemicals such as methane (CH4), methanol (CH3OH), and ethylene (C2H4), in a green and sustainable manner [1, 2]. With the rapid expansion in the field of renewable energy, especially renewable electricity generation, electrocatalytic CO2 conversion provides us a feasible pathway to reach practical application of CO2 conversion. To this end, numerous catalysts have been investigated for electrocatalytic CO2 conversion, and Cu is found to be the most promosing metal that can convert CO2 into multi-carbon products with a prominent efficiency and selectivity [3, 4].
Recently, it has been extensively reported that the structural and chemical states of the Cu surface have shown dynamic
changes in response to the local environment and applied potential during the electrocatalytic process [5]. In particular, surface reconstruction is an inevitable phenomenon owing to the low cohesive energy and high surface mobility of Cu atoms. It has been reported that the proper control of the surface reconstruction can lead to the formation of high-index facets on Cu and enhance the catalytic performance of the Cu [6–8]. For example, Choi et al. reported that the surface reconstruction of the Cu nanoparticles during the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction can cause the formation of high-index facets, leading to the high selectivity toward C2H4 [9]. However, some previous reports also indicate that the adsorption energies of *CO and *CO2− are relatively low on {100} facets of Cu, allowing {100} facets to be more favorable for the production of C2H4 [6]. Considering such a discrepancy, it is of significance to track the preferable surface active sites on Cu for C2H4 production, enabling a throughout understanding of the influence of surface reconstruction on the electrocatalytic performance.
To this end, the meticulous design of the Cu surface through

surface reconstruction holds the key to provide an ideal platform for the study of this issue. In past decades, the Cu nanoparticles derived from Cu compounds such as Cu2O, CuxS, and Cu3N have demonstrated their immense potential in the field of electrocatalytic CO2 conversion [10–13]. Among the compounds, owing to the complexity of crystal structure and high mobility of S atoms in copper sulfide crystals, Cu2−xS can be a perfect precursor to prepare the high-index faceted Cu nanoparticles through surface reconstruction for electrocatalytic CO2 conversion [14, 15]. Here we prepared polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles (denoted as Cu-s) derived from Cu2−xS for the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. It is revealed that the surface reconstruction of the Cu2−xS derived Cu nanoparticles during the electrocatalytic reaction can allow the formation of the high-index facets, which are advantageous for promoting the formation of C2H4. In addition, according to the operando Raman spectroscopy, the adsorbed *COCHO has been confirmed to be the major intermediate for the production of C2H4. This work is expected to deepen the understanding of the construction of Cu nanoparticles with high-index facets through the surface reconstruction and their corresponding electrocatalytic CO2 reduction mechanism.

sections.heading: 2 Results and discussion
sections.text:
In this work, Cu2−xS nanocrystals were first synthesized by the reaction of copper chloride with di-tert-butyl disulfide (TBDS) in an oleylamine solution under 200 °C [16, 17]. The formation of roxbyite Cu2−xS was confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Fig. S1 in the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM)), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Fig. S2 in the ESM) and Cu LMM Auger electron spectroscopy (AES, Fig. S3 in the ESM). Furthermore, transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Fig. 1(a)) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Fig. 1(b)) reveal that the Cu2−xS nanocrystals have a uniform size of 80–100 nm. The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image (Fig. 1(c)) further demonstrates that the lattice fringes of Cu2−xS nanocrystals are 0.309 and 0.282 nm, which can be assigned to the (1010) and (107) planes of roxbyite Cu2−xS phase, respectively [18]. To benchmark the performance, the commercial copper nanoparticles (denoted as Cu-c) were also employed as the controlled group. As shown
in Fig. 1(d), the size of Cu-c is in the range of 150–200 nm. The electrocatalytic CO2 conversion reaction was conducted using a typical H-type cell and CO2 was purged into 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte continuously with a flow rate of 20 sccm during the reaction. The gaseous and liquid products were separately collected from the reactor every 20 min and analyzed by gas chromatograph and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2(a), the major product from electrocatalytic CO2 conversion using Cu2−xS at the initial stage is formic acid (HCOOH). This feature is typically induced by the presence of S atoms in Cu lattice that can significantly reduce Gibbs free energy for the formation of HCOO*, the prime intermediate for the production of HCOOH [19, 20]. At this stage, Cu2−xS is expected to be reduced into Cu-s due to the dislodging of the S elements during the electrochemical reaction. Beyond this stage, the Faradic efficiency (FE) of C2H4 gradually increases as the reaction proceeds and reaches a stable value of around 68.8% after 2 h of reaction. More importantly, such a high FE of C2H4 remains almost unchanged (within ±5%) for subsequent 5 h of reaction. This indicates that the desulphurization and surface reconstruction have been completed to form stable catalytic structures (denoted as Cu-s) within the first 2 h.
To demonstrate the electrocatalytic performance of Cu-s, the potential-dependent FEs were measured after the formation of Cu-s as shown in Fig. 2(b). At an applied potential of −1.2 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), Cu-s reaches the maximum FE of C2H4 (69.3%). With further increasing applied potential, the FE of C2H4 decreases and the relatively low-value CO and HCOOH turn as the major products, indicating that dimerization

of intermediate can hardly occur at a relatively positive potential. For the Cu-c (Fig. 2(c)), the FEs of C2H4 and HCOOH are low irrespective of the applied potential and the reaction duration. To estimate the CO2 conversion efficiency on the prepared samples, the partial current densities of Cu-s (Fig. 2(d)) and Cu-c (Fig. 2(e)) are also calculated. Compared with Cu-c, Cu-s exhibits higher total current density and partial current density for C2H4 across the entire applied potential range (from −1.3 to −0.9 V vs. RHE). With an applied potential of −1.2 V vs. RHE, the partial current density of C2H4 for Cu-s reaches the highest value of 35.4 mA/cm2, which is two times higher than that of Cu-c, suggesting its superior C2H4 production efficiency. According to the long-term chronoamperometry I–t curve of Cu-s (Fig. S4 in the ESM), the Cu-s shows negligible current delay after 8 h of electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction, indicating an excellent stability of electrocatalyst.
Upon acquiring the outstanding performance of Cu-s, we recognized the prodigious improvement of C2H4 FE during the electroreduction of Cu2−xS into Cu-s (i.e., the first 2 h in Fig. 2(a)). The question naturally arises what factors induce such a remarkable performance improvement during the formation of the final Cu-s structure. To this end, we analyzed the structure of Cu-s to answer the question. We first collected the samples after electroreduction reaction for different durations (10 min and 2 h) by ultrasonication and their TEM and HRTEM images were taken. For the sample collected at 10 min of electroreduction, the lattice fringes of the polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles were measured to be 0.208 and 0.180 nm (see Figs. S5(a) and S5(b) in the ESM), which can be indexed to the (111) and (200) plane of face-centered cubic (fcc) Cu, respectively. This result is an indication that most of the Cu2−xS nanocrystals have been transformed into polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles. Only a small portion of Cu2−xS nanocrystals remain after 10 min of electroreduction, suggesting the rapid transformation of the Cu2−xS nanocrystals into Cu nanoparticles. For the sample collected at 2 h of electroreduction, the polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles are highly aggregated and the Cu2−xS nanocrystals mostly disappear (see Figs. S5(c), S5(d) and S6 in the ESM). The above observation reveals that the sample significantly changes during the electroreduction with an applied potential of −1.2 V vs. RHE. At the initial stage of the reaction, the Cu2−xS starts to be reduced along with the dislodging of S atoms into the electrolyte, resulting in the collapse of the Cu2−xS lattice and the formation of Cu-s. According to the previous reports [6, 21], the surface reconstruction will take place after the formation of Cu-s and continuously proceed with the evolution of the electroreduction duration.
Considering that this surface reconstruction can be the main reason for the enhanced electrocatalytic CO2 conversion into the C2H4, we employed in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) to track the change of the sample during the process. As revealed by the Cu K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra (Fig. 3(a) and Fig. S7 in the ESM)
and corresponding k2-weighted Fourier-transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) spectra (Fig. 3(b)), the signal of Cu2−xS disappears after 2 min of electroreduction reaction. Furthermore, a peak at 2.23 Å attributed to the coordination of Cu–Cu simultaneously arises with the disappearance of Cu2−xS, suggesting the transformation of Cu2−xS into the metallic Cu. It should be noted that no noticeable changes can be observed during the subsequent electroreduction reaction (8–60 min). Therefore, the crystal structure change is certainly not the main reason for the superior performance of the Cu2−xS derived Cu after electroreduction for 2 h.
Given the exclusion of the influence of crystal structure changes on the CO2 conversion performance, we thus look into the subtler factors—surface structures of the Cu nanoparticles. Therewith, we performed the OH− adsorption measurements to correlate the surface structures of Cu-s to the electrocatalytic performance [9, 22]. The resistance of the catalyst during the LSV test remains nearly unchanged in the range of 0.250.42 V vs. RHE so that linear background can be subtracted from the OH− adsorption spectra (see original spectra in Fig. S8 in the ESM). Compared with the OH− adsorption on Cu2−xS, the Cu-s shows three extra OH− adsorption peaks. In detail, the peaks at around 0.362 and 0.395 V vs. RHE are assigned to the Cu(OH) adsorption peaks on Cu {100} and Cu {110}, respectively [11]. In addition, the third peak at the most negative applied potential is ascribed to the high-index facet of copper (denoted as S-{hkl}), which owns the extremely high surface energy and abundant coordinatively unsaturated Cu atoms for promoting electrocatalytic CO2 reaction [23–25]. More importantly, as shown in Figs. 4(a)–4(d), the ratio of S-{hkl} increases with the evolution of reaction time. Specifically, the ratio of S-{hkl} increases from 35.6% to 83.6% with the evolution of time from 20 to 100 min. Such an increase in the ratio of S-{hkl} is in good agreement with the trend of C2H4 production efficiency

4
enhancement (see Table S1 in the ESM and Fig. 4(f)). It should be noted that the ratio of {100} facets decreases from 41.2% to 7.1%. Such a result clearly demonstrates that the above enhanced C2H4 production performance of the Cu stems from the {hkl} facets instead of the {100} facets. To confirm this assertion, we performed the OH− adsorption test using the Cu-c as the reference. As shown in Fig. 4(e) and Fig. S9 in the ESM, the intensity of the Cu(OH) peak increases with the evolution of reaction time, but the ratio of high-index facets remains low and there is no significant change in the position of the peak with the prolonging of reaction time, suggesting the negligible surface property change of Cu-c during the electrocatalytic reaction. Therefore, trivial enhancement in the performance of Cu-c can be observed with the evolution of electrocatalytic reaction duration.
Based on these results, it can be conclusively confirmed that the crystal structure and surface properties of Cu2−xS are drastically altered during the process of transformation and the formation of the high-index S-{hkl) through the surface reconstruction plays the dominant role in determining the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction performance. In detail, Cu2−xS undergoes a two-step transformation during the electroreduction as illustrated in Scheme 1. In the first step (electroreduction for 0–10 min), Cu2−xS nanoparticles are desulphurized and transformed into Cu nanoparticles. Attributed to the presence of S elements in the Cu lattice, the major product of the CO2 reduction reaction is HCOOH in this step. In the second step, the sample undergoes the surface reconstruction, where the polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles derived from Cu2−xS nanocrystals aggregate gradually, along with the formation of high-index facets [16]. Together with the increase in the ratio of highindex facets, the major product of the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction for Cu-s alters from the C1 (HCOOH) to C2 (C2H4) products, suggesting the dominant role of high-index facets in determining product distribution.
After the determination of active sites on Cu-s, we then assessed the electrocatalytic CO2 conversion mechanism for Cu-s. Although *CO is known as the most important intermediate for the CO2 reduction reaction [26], it is imperative to discern the detailed dimerization and protonation pathway of *CO toward the production of C2 compounds on the Cu-s. Generally, there are two possible C–C coupling pathways for *CO [27, 28], including *COCOH pathway and *COCHO pathway.
*COCOH pathway:
2*CO → *COCO (1) *COCO + *H → *COCOH (2)
*COCHO pathway:
*CO + *H → *CHO (3) *CHO + *CO → *COCHO (4)
Given that the main difference between these two intermediate species is their positions of H atoms, the detection of C–H and O–H bonds can be the clue to determine the major intermediate products. From this perspective, we performed the operando Raman spectroscopy during the electrocatalytic CO2 conversion using Cu-c and Cu-s at different applied potentials to examine the state of the intermediate species. As shown in
  Scheme 1 Schematic illustration for the transformation from Cu2−xS to Cu-s.
Fig. 5, two peaks attributed to the carbon of glassy carbon electrode at 1,335 and 1,650 cm−1 can be observed, and the peak at 1,335 cm−1 is used as an indicator to normalize other peaks. For the test using Cu-c, the peak at 2,060–2,080 cm−1, assigned to C–O stretching mode of *CO, appears at −0.5 V vs. RHE and the peak intensity gradually increases with the applied potential decreasing to −0.7 V vs. RHE. By further decreasing the applied potential, this peak disappears, suggesting that the *CO intermediate can either transform into other species or desorb from the Cu surface. Such a result is in good accordance with the above performance test of Cu-c, where the FEs of C2H4 and CO obviously increase as the potential decreases.
In contrast, no peak attributed to *CO can be found on the operando Raman spectroscopy using Cu-s (see Fig. 5(a)) throughout the test, underscoring the rapid reaction of the *CO with other surface functional groups. In addition, a strong peak at 2,700 cm−1 attributed to the C–H stretching mode of aldehydes (*CHO) can be observed. Such a position of the C–H stretching mode of aldehydes is distinct from that of the commonly observed C–H stretching mode at 2,800–3,200 cm−1 because the extremely electronegative behavior of the oxygen in C=O can reduce the electron density of C–H bond of *CHO and cause the abatement of its Raman position to 2,600–2,850 cm−1. During the subsequent reaction, *CHO can be either directly reduced into CH4 or coupled with *CO to form *COCHO. Given that the kinetic barrier (0.46 eV) for coupling of *CO and *CHO is lower than that (0.59 eV) of reduction of *CHO on the S-{hkl} [9], the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction using Cu-s should follow the *COCHO pathway.

sections.heading: 3 Conclusion
sections.text: In conclusion, we have successfully prepared the polycrystalline Cu nanoparticles derived from Cu2−xS nanocrystals with rich high-index facets, providing a platform for evaluating the contribution of surface construction to electrocatalytic CO2 conversion. It is discovered that the emergence of high-index facets during the surface reconstruction is beneficial to endow surface active sites for the C–C coupling, thereby enhancing the production of the C2H4. In addition, according to the operando Raman spectroscopy, we reveal that the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction using Cu-s follows the *COCHO pathway to produce C2H4. Our findings highlight the importance of the structure–activity relationship of Cu electrocatalysts and provide new insights into the fabrication of advanced electrocatalytic CO2 reduction systems toward C2+ compound production.
